set.detail:
The Roman story is a drama in three acts. Tarquinius Superbus is besieging Ardea when his sons and their cousin L. Tarquinius Collatinus, bored in camp, wager on whose wife is the most virtuous; riding home at night they find the princesses at a banquet and Collatinus' Lucretia spinning wool among her maids. Sextus Tarquinius returns days later, rapes her at sword-point by threatening to kill her beside a dead slave, and Lucretia summons her father Sp. Lucretius and her husband, who come with P. Valerius and L. Junius Brutus. She tells them what happened and stabs herself. Brutus, who had feigned stupidity (brutus, 'dullard') to survive the king's purges, draws the knife from her body and swears to drive out the Tarquins and never again suffer a king at Rome. The body is displayed in the forum of Collatia and then in Rome; the people vote the king's deposition, Brutus wins over the army at Ardea, Queen Tullia flees, and Tarquin finds the gates shut and goes into exile at Caere. Sextus is killed at Gabii.

Livy and Dionysius tell the tale with deliberate echoes of Athenian history: in 510 the Peisistratids were expelled after a sexual insult provoked Harmodius and Aristogeiton, and Roman annalists consciously aligned the two liberations. The Varronian date of 509 puts the event 244 years after the foundation; Polybius dates the first consuls 28 years before Xerxes' invasion, which gives 508/507. What can be checked supports a date around 500: the monarchy's sacral functions survived in the rex sacrorum and the Regifugium ritual of 24 February, the Capitoline temple was dedicated in the first year of the new regime, the Carthage treaty presupposes a Rome that still claimed Tarquin's Latin hegemony, and the Fasti, whatever their early distortions, begin then.

Modern debate concerns the how rather than the whether. Alföldi and Gjerstad argued for a later date (c. 470 or 450) on archaeological grounds now largely abandoned. Many scholars think Lars Porsenna, not a Roman aristocratic coup, ended Tarquin's rule, and that the transition passed through a phase of chief magistrates (praetor maximus, dictator) before annual collegial consuls became fixed. The result, in any case, was an aristocratic republic whose ideology was built on hatred of the name rex: Caesar's enemies in 44 BC would invoke Brutus at his statue on the Capitol.

scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) ch. 9
Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965)

set.detail:
Livy says the first two consuls were elected by the centuriate assembly 'according to the commentaries of Servius Tullius', and that they received all the king's powers and insignia except that only one held the fasces at a time, alternating month by month so that the people would not see two kings. Brutus made the people swear never to allow a king, and Valerius added the right of appeal (provocatio). The office was annual and collegial, each consul able to veto the other; it carried imperium, the power of command and coercion, and the auspicia, the right to consult the gods on the state's behalf.

Our main documentary source, the Fasti Capitolini compiled under Augustus from earlier lists, credits 509 with five consuls: Brutus and Collatinus, then Sp. Lucretius (who died in office), Valerius and M. Horatius. The crowding betrays later reconstruction, and Polybius' treaty, which names Brutus and Horatius, does not match the traditional pairs of 509. Livy himself notes that the chief magistrates were at first called praetors, and an old law on the Capitol ordered the 'praetor maximus' to drive the annual nail; Festus explains praetor maximus as the senior of several. Scholars such as De Martino and Mazzarino therefore suggested that the Republic began with a single annual chief magistrate, or with a dictator-like praetor maximus assisted by junior colleagues, and that two equal consuls emerged only in 449 or even 367. Others, following Cornell, accept the dual magistracy from the start but agree that its title was praetor until the 4th century.

The early Fasti also contain many non-patrician names (Cassius, Genucius, Minucius, Sempronius, Volumnius): about a third of the consuls of 509-486 bear names later known as plebeian. This has fuelled the theory of a 'closing of the patriciate' (serrata) in the 5th century, when a narrower group monopolised office, against which the plebeian struggle was directed. The consular year began on varying dates until 153, when 1 January was fixed. Dating by consular pairs, the habit that made the Fasti the backbone of Roman chronology, began with this office.

The temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, with Juno and Minerva in side chambers, was the central monument of Roman religion and politics. Tradition said Tarquinius Priscus vowed it in a Sabine war and levelled the summit, Tarquinius Superbus built it with Etruscan craftsmen, financing it from the spoils of Suessa Pometia, and the gods Terminus and Iuventas refused to leave the site, an omen of permanence. The terracotta cult statue of Jupiter, painted red with minium, and the quadriga on the roof were commissioned from Vulca of Veii, the only named Etruscan artist known from Roman literature. On the Ides of September of the first year, the consul M. Horatius Pulvillus dedicated it; told mid-ceremony that his son had died, he kept his hand on the doorpost and finished the prayer.

The building was huge. Excavations under Palazzo Caffarelli and in the Capitoline Museums (Mura Sommella, 1998-2000s) have exposed foundations of cappellaccio tufa measuring roughly 54 by 62 m, larger than any other temple of the 6th century west of Greece except the Sicilian giants. Its Tuscan plan, with a deep columned porch and three cellae on a high podium, became the model for Roman temples in Italy and the provinces, and its dedication date became an era: an old law said the praetor maximus should fix a nail in the wall on the Ides of September, and Pliny dates Cn. Flavius' shrine of Concord 204 years after the dedication. Triumphs ended there, consuls sacrificed there on taking office, and the Senate met there at the start of the year.

The original temple burned in 83 BC and was rebuilt by Sulla and Q. Lutatius Catulus (dedicated 69 BC) on the old plan; it burned again in AD 69 and 80 and was rebuilt by Vespasian and Domitian. Debate continues over whether the vast foundations carried a temple of the same size or a smaller building on a broad platform, and whether the scale reflects Tarquin's ambition or later enlargement. Either way, the dedication in 509 or 507 shows that the expulsion of the kings did not interrupt the great building programme of archaic Rome.
set.debate: Dedication in 509 or 507 is disputed in antiquity; modern debate concerns the reconstruction of the superstructure on the 54 x 62 m foundations.

scholarship: A. Mura Sommella, 'Il tempio di Giove Capitolino', Mitteilungen des DAI Rom 2008
Hopkins, The Genesis of Roman Architecture (2016)

set.detail:
Polybius found the treaty in the treasury of the aediles beside the Capitoline temple, engraved on bronze, in Latin so archaic that the best experts could barely understand it, and he gives a Greek paraphrase. It dates, he says, to the consulship of L. Junius Brutus and M. Horatius, 28 years before Xerxes crossed to Greece. Its terms: there shall be friendship between the Romans and their allies and the Carthaginians and theirs. The Romans shall not sail beyond the Fair Promontory unless forced by storm or enemies; if forced, they may take only what is needed for repairs or sacrifice and must leave within five days. Merchants trading in Libya or Sardinia may do business only in the presence of a herald or scribe, and the state guarantees the price. In the part of Sicily ruled by Carthage, Romans have equal rights. The Carthaginians shall not harm Ardea, Antium, Laurentum, Circeii, Tarracina or any other Latin city subject to Rome; if they take a Latin city not subject to Rome, they must hand it over undamaged; they shall build no fort in Latium, and if they enter it in arms shall not spend a night there.

The treaty is the single most important document for early Rome. It shows a Rome claiming hegemony over the coastal Latin cities as far as Tarracina, as Livy says Tarquin had held, and a Carthage already organising exclusive trading zones, with the 'Fair Promontory' (probably Cape Farina, north of Carthage, or less likely Cape Bon) marking the closed waters of the Gulf of Tunis and the coast beyond. It parallels the Etrusco-Punic agreements known from Aristotle and the Pyrgi tablets.

Mommsen and many 19th-century scholars rejected the date and identified it with the treaty of 348 mentioned by Diodorus and Livy, which Diodorus calls the first. Most modern historians (Scullard, Walbank, Cornell) accept Polybius: the archaic language, the Latin cities named and the absence of the restrictions of 348 all fit c. 509. The treaties of 348, 306 (if Philinus' version is accepted) and 279 followed, and Polybius cited the series to judge responsibility for the First Punic War.

scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 337-345

set.detail:
In Livy's patriotic narrative Lars Porsenna, king of Clusium, marched on Rome to restore Tarquin. He seized the Janiculum in a rush, and only Horatius Cocles, with Sp. Larcius and T. Herminius, held the far end of the Pons Sublicius while the Romans hacked it down behind them; Horatius then swam the Tiber in full armour. The blockade that followed caused famine. The young noble C. Mucius slipped into the Etruscan camp to kill the king, stabbed his secretary by mistake, and, when threatened with torture, thrust his right hand into a brazier, telling Porsenna that 300 young Romans had sworn to try in turn; he was released and took the name Scaevola, 'Lefty'. Porsenna made peace, receiving hostages and the return of the seven pagi on the right bank taken from Veii. The hostage Cloelia escaped across the Tiber with other girls; returned by Rome under the treaty, she was freed by the admiring king with half the hostages, and an equestrian statue of her stood on the Via Sacra.

Other evidence tells a different story. Tacitus, describing the burning of the Capitol in AD 69, says the temple had survived 'when the city was surrendered' (dedita urbe) to Porsenna. Pliny quotes the treaty with Porsenna, which forbade the Romans to use iron except for agriculture, a typical condition imposed on a defeated people. Dionysius records that Rome sent Porsenna a throne, sceptre and crown, tokens of submission. The custom at Roman auctions of announcing 'the goods of King Porsenna for sale' was explained by Livy as a memory of the king's generosity in leaving his camp's supplies.

Most modern scholars conclude that Porsenna took Rome. Whether he came to restore Tarquin or to replace him is unclear; some suggest he removed Tarquin himself and that the Roman aristocracy seized power when his son Arruns was defeated by the Latins and Aristodemus of Cumae at Aricia (504). The heroic stories are aetiologies for monuments (the statues of Cloelia and Horatius) and family names. The Clusine king's legendary tomb, a labyrinth crowned by pyramids described by Varro, shows how large he loomed in Etruscan memory.

scholarship: Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965) 72-84

set.detail:
After the Tarquins' last hope in Etruria faded, the Latin cities under Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum, Tarquin's son-in-law, went to war with Rome, sheltering the old king. The Senate appointed A. Postumius Albus dictator with T. Aebutius Elva as master of horse. The armies met at Lake Regillus in the territory of Tusculum, probably the drained crater of Pantano Secco below Frascati. Livy describes a heroic battle of leaders in Homeric style: the aged Tarquin, charging Postumius, was wounded; Aebutius and Mamilius wounded each other; Mamilius was finally killed by T. Herminius, himself slain moments later; the Roman exiles' cohort under Tarquin's son fought ferociously. Postumius ordered the cavalry to dismount and fight on foot, vowed a temple to Castor, and promised rewards to the first men over the Latin camp's rampart.

Later tradition added that two tall youths on white horses fought at the head of the Roman cavalry, and that the same evening two horsemen were seen washing their mounts at the spring of Juturna in the Forum, announcing the victory before vanishing: Castor and Pollux. Their temple beside the spring was dedicated by Postumius' son in 484, and the annual parade of the equites on 15 July (transvectio equitum), reorganised by Q. Fabius Rullianus in 304, commemorated the battle's anniversary.

The Dioscuri were Greek gods, but an inscribed bronze from Lavinium of the late 6th century (Castorei Podlouqueique qurois) shows they were already worshipped in Latium, perhaps as patrons of aristocratic cavalry. Livy noted that his sources dated the battle to 499 or 496. The outcome was less decisive than the legend: the Foedus Cassianum of 493 created an alliance of equals rather than Roman supremacy, and Tusculum later became Rome's closest Latin friend. Macaulay's 'Battle of the Lake Regillus' in his Lays of Ancient Rome (1842) made the story famous to Victorian readers.
set.debate: Date (499 or 496), site of the lake, and the decisiveness of the victory are disputed; the Dioscuri epiphany is an aetiological legend tied to the Juturna spring and the transvectio.

scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 285-291
Weinstock, 'Two Archaic Inscriptions from Latium', JRS 50 (1960)

set.detail:
Debt bondage (nexum), harsh debt judgments and the burden of continual war produced the crisis. When the consuls of 494 tried to march out the legions, still bound by their military oath, the soldiers instead withdrew in arms to the Mons Sacer, a hill beyond the Anio three miles from Rome, though the annalist Piso placed the secession on the Aventine. They camped peacefully for some days while the patricians, fearing both the plebs inside the city and enemies outside, negotiated. Menenius Agrippa, himself of plebeian origin according to Livy, told the fable of the limbs that starved the belly and found they starved themselves, a story that already existed in Greek literature.

The settlement created the tribunes of the plebs: two at first, by Livy's account C. Licinius and L. Albinus, who co-opted three more including L. Sicinius, the leader of the secession; other versions name five from the start. The tribunes' power rested not on law but on the sworn oath of the whole plebs (lex sacrata) to kill anyone who harmed them: they were sacrosanct. Their function was auxilium, protecting individual plebeians against magistrates, which grew into a general veto (intercessio). Plebeian aediles and the cult centre of Ceres, Liber and Libera on the Aventine slope followed.

Modern historians see the secession as the birth of a 'state within the state', with its own assembly, officers, archive and treasury, a model unparalleled in the Greek world. Who the plebs were is debated: not simply the poor, since wealthy plebeians led the movement, and perhaps not originally including the patricians' clients. The secession, a military strike, became the plebs' ultimate weapon, repeated in 449, in the mutiny of 342 and in the final secession to the Janiculum in 287. The story's details are later reconstructions, often coloured by the tribunician politics of the Gracchan age, but the creation of the tribunate early in the 5th century is generally accepted.

scholarship: Raaflaub (ed.), Social Struggles in Archaic Rome (2nd ed. 2005)

set.detail:
After Lake Regillus the consul Sp. Cassius made a treaty with the Latin cities that defined relations in Latium for 150 years. Dionysius gives its text: there shall be peace between the Romans and all the Latin cities as long as heaven and earth keep their place; they shall not make war on one another, nor bring in enemies, nor give them passage; each shall help the other with all its strength when attacked; each shall have an equal share of the spoils of joint wars; private lawsuits shall be decided within ten days in the city where the contract was made; and nothing shall be added or removed except by agreement of Romans and Latins together. Cicero says the treaty was engraved on a bronze column behind the Rostra and had been seen there not long before his time. Festus preserves an archaic clause about booty (pecuniam quis nancitor habeto).

The command of joint armies probably alternated: Cincius, quoted by Festus, describes the Latins meeting at the spring of Ferentina to decide on years when a Roman commander would lead them. Shared rights, later called Latin rights, allowed intermarriage (conubium), legally valid trade and contracts (commercium) and the right to migrate and take up citizenship (ius migrandi). Joint Latin colonies were planted on the frontiers: Signia, Velitrae, Norba, Ardea, Satricum, Setia, Circeii, Sutrium and Nepet. The Hernici joined the system in 486.

Scholars disagree on how equal the alliance was. Dionysius' text presents a bilateral treaty between Rome and 'the Latins' as one party, and some think Rome was already the dominant partner, as the first Carthage treaty implies. The alliance held through the Volscian and Aequian wars of the 5th century, frayed after the Gallic sack, was renewed in 358, and ended in the revolt of 340 when the Latins demanded one consul and half the Senate. Its rights and obligations became the template for the status of Latin colonies across Italy and, through the ius Latii, for provincial communities under the Empire.

After a decade of tribunician agitation for written law, the patricians agreed in 452 to a codification, provided the codifiers were patricians. For 451 the consulship and the tribunate were suspended and ten men were elected 'for writing the laws' (decemviri legibus scribundis) with consular power and no appeal: Ap. Claudius and T. Genucius, the consuls-designate, the three envoys sent to Greece, and five others. Livy says they governed with moderation, each in turn holding the fasces for a day while his colleagues were attended only by an orderly, and that Appius was the dominant figure. At year's end they displayed ten tables in the Forum and invited citizens to propose amendments, after which the laws were passed by the centuriate assembly.

The embassy of 454, which supposedly studied the laws of Solon at Athens and other Greek cities, is controversial. The Twelve Tables do contain rules with clear Greek parallels: Gaius compared the rule on boundary spaces to a law of Solon, the rule on associations to another, and Cicero noted that the limits on funeral luxury were borrowed from Solon. Pliny says Hermodorus of Ephesus, an exile who advised the decemvirs, was honoured with a statue in the Comitium. Many scholars think the Greek influence came through Magna Graecia, especially Cumae and the law codes of Zaleucus and Charondas, rather than from Athens directly.

The first decemvirate was so satisfactory, according to Livy, that a second board was elected for 450 to complete the work, with fatal results. The suspension of the tribunate shows that the plebs had accepted giving up their protective office in exchange for written law, a sign of how much they valued certainty against patrician arbitrariness.
set.debate: The historicity of the embassy to Athens and the extent of Greek influence on the code are debated; some doubt that the tribunate was really suspended.

set.detail:
The Twelve Tables were Rome's first and only comprehensive codification before Justinian. Ten tables were enacted in 451 and two more in 450; they were displayed in the Forum, on bronze according to Livy, on wood or ivory according to other writers, and are said to have perished in the Gallic sack. The text survives only in quotations by Cicero, Festus, Gellius, the jurists and Gaius' lost commentary, and modern reconstructions (the standard edition is Crawford's Roman Statutes no. 40) assign fragments to tables by guesswork.

The fragments are terse commands in archaic Latin. 'If he summons to court, let him go' (si in ius vocat, ito) opens the code. A judgment debtor had thirty days' grace; then the creditor could lay hands on him, take him home in chains for sixty days, display him at three market days, and then, the code says, 'cut shares' (partes secanto) among several creditors or sell him abroad across the Tiber. A father who sold his son three times lost his power over him, a clause later used as a fiction for emancipation. Possession of land for two years and of other things for one gave ownership (usucapio); a wife who stayed away three nights a year avoided falling into her husband's power (manus). Breaking a free man's bone cost 300 asses, a slave's 150; a simple insult 25; maiming was punished by retaliation unless settled. A thief caught at night could be killed; a false witness was thrown from the Tarpeian Rock; a patron who defrauded his client was declared sacer. No one was to be buried or cremated inside the city, women were not to tear their cheeks at funerals, and gold was not to be buried with the dead, except gold binding the teeth. Magical spells against crops or persons were capital, and capital cases could be decided only by the 'greatest assembly'.

The code was not a constitution but a statement of existing custom on procedure, family, property, debt and delict, removing it from pontifical secrecy. Livy called it 'the fount of all public and private law', and Cicero recalled learning it by heart as a boy. Its authenticity, doubted by Pais and Lambert, is now accepted on linguistic grounds, and its picture of an agrarian society of farmers, debtors, clients and slaves is our best window on 5th-century Rome.
set.debate: The text is a modern reconstruction; the attribution of fragments to individual tables and some clauses (e.g. the literal cutting of debtors) are disputed.

scholarship: Watson, Rome of the XII Tables (1975)

set.detail:
The second decemvirate, re-elected in 450 with Appius Claudius at its head, ruled beyond its term into 449 with 120 lictors and axes in the fasces, according to Livy. While two armies fought the Sabines and the Aequi, Appius conceived a passion for Verginia, daughter of the plebeian centurion L. Verginius and betrothed of the former tribune L. Icilius. He had his client M. Claudius claim her in court as the child of one of his slave women, and then, as judge, awarded interim custody to the claimant, violating the decemvirs' own rule that liberty should be presumed pending trial. Verginius, summoned from the army on the Algidus, led his daughter aside near the shrine of Cloacina in the Forum, seized a butcher's knife from a stall and stabbed her, crying that this was the only way to keep her free.

He rode to the army, which marched to Rome and occupied the Aventine; the Sabine army, roused by Icilius and Numitorius, joined it. When the decemvirs refused to resign, the plebs withdrew to the Mons Sacer, leaving the city empty. The Senate sent L. Valerius and M. Horatius to negotiate; the decemvirs abdicated, tribunes were elected on the Aventine (including Verginius, Icilius and Numitorius), and Valerius and Horatius were elected consuls and carried their famous laws. Appius killed himself in prison awaiting trial.

The Verginia story closely mirrors that of Lucretia: an act of sexual violence by a tyrant against a virtuous woman, a male relative's sacrifice, and the overthrow of the oppressor. It is a moral drama about liberty (libertas) and the protection of the citizen body, with the legal point of vindiciae secundum libertatem at its centre. Modern historians treat the details as legend. Some argue that the image of a tyrannical second decemvirate is itself a construction to explain why the last two tables included the unpopular ban on patrician-plebeian intermarriage, and that the reforms attributed to 449 were partly retrojected from later centuries.
set.debate: The tyranny of the second decemvirate and the Verginia story are widely seen as legend modelled on Lucretia; the extent of the 449 restoration is debated.

scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 476-500

set.detail:
The consuls of the restoration, L. Valerius Potitus and M. Horatius Barbatus, carried three laws in the centuriate assembly that Livy presents as the charter of plebeian liberty. First, what the plebs resolved in its tribal assembly (plebiscitum) should bind the whole people. Second, no one should create a magistracy without appeal (provocatio), and anyone who did so might be killed without crime. Third, the tribunes of the plebs, the plebeian aediles and 'the judges, the decemvirs' were declared sacrosanct by statute, anyone harming them to be sacer to Jupiter and his property sold at the temple of Ceres. The tribune M. Duillius then carried a plebiscite threatening flogging and beheading for anyone who left the plebs without tribunes or created a magistrate without appeal. The consuls also began the practice of depositing copies of senatorial decrees with the plebeian aediles at the temple of Ceres, to prevent the patricians from altering them.

The first law poses a famous puzzle. Livy credits the same rule to Q. Publilius Philo in 339 and to the dictator Q. Hortensius in 287, and only the last is universally accepted as decisive. Explanations include: the 449 law required senatorial approval (auctoritas patrum) for plebiscites, and 339 and 287 progressively removed conditions; the 449 law referred to the tribal assembly of the whole people (comitia tributa) rather than the plebeian council; or the 449 and 339 laws are annalistic doublets. The second law similarly duplicates the leges Valeriae de provocatione of 509 and 300, the latter generally regarded as the first genuine one.

Whatever their exact content, the laws of 449 mark the moment when the plebeian institutions created by oath in 494 began to be recognised by the state as a whole. The Valerii and Horatii appear in the tradition as the patrician houses friendly to the plebs, a pattern that owes much to family historians such as Valerius Antias.

scholarship: Lintott, The Constitution of the Roman Republic (1999) 33-37

set.detail:
In 445 the tribune C. Canuleius proposed that patricians and plebeians be allowed to intermarry, repealing the clause of the last two tables, while his colleagues proposed that one consul might be plebeian. The patricians objected that mixed marriages would confuse the gentes and pollute the auspices, which only patricians could take, since children of a mixed marriage would not know to which order they belonged. Livy gives Canuleius a celebrated speech: Rome's kings themselves had been outsiders, Numa a Sabine, Tarquinius Priscus the son of a Corinthian exile, Servius Tullius the son of a captive woman; why should a plebeian not marry a patrician or hold the consulship if the people elected him? The marriage law passed; the consulship proposal was deflected by the creation of military tribunes with consular power in 444.

The consequences were long-term rather than immediate. Intermarriage allowed the formation of a mixed elite of patrician and wealthy plebeian families, linked by marriage alliances, that became the nobilitas of the 4th and 3rd centuries. Because patrician status passed through the father, plebeian men who married patrician women did not change their children's status, which explains episodes like the story of Fabia (377) and Verginia's shrine of Plebeian Chastity (296).

Scholars disagree about what was banned. Cicero says the decemvirs added the prohibition to the last two tables, but many think patricians had long been endogamous by custom, and that the decemvirs only codified it. Others suggest the ban concerned the sacral form of marriage (confarreatio) required for certain priesthoods, rather than all unions. Whether there was real social mixing before 445 is uncertain: the plebeian names among the early consuls suggest a more open early elite, which had closed by the mid-5th century and was now reopened.
set.debate: Whether the decemvirs introduced a new ban or codified patrician endogamy, and whether the ban applied to all marriage or only confarreatio, are debated.

scholarship: Linderski, 'The Auspices and the Struggle of the Orders', in Eder (ed.), Staat und Staatlichkeit (1990)

set.detail:
From 444 to 367 Rome was governed in most years not by two consuls but by a college of military tribunes with consular power (tribuni militum consulari potestate): three in the early years, four in some, and six from 405 onward. Livy counts about fifty such years. The first college of 444 abdicated after three months because of a flaw in their election, and suffect consuls took over, which Licinius Macer confirmed from the treaty with Ardea and the linen books.

Ancient writers offered two explanations, both recorded by Livy. The political one: the patricians, under pressure from the Canuleian agitation, created an office that plebeians could hold without opening the consulship itself. The military one: Rome needed more commanders than two consuls to fight the Aequi, Volsci and Veii at once. The facts fit the second better. No plebeian was elected until P. Licinius Calvus in 400, after which plebeians appear frequently, and the larger colleges of six coincide with the multi-front wars of 405-396 and the 380s. Consular tribunes never triumphed, suggesting that their auspices or imperium differed from the consuls'. Modern scholars (for example Cornell, Ridley, Bastien) generally combine the explanations: a flexible military command structure that also became an arena of plebeian ambition.

The years without consuls (375-371) belong to the same period and are now thought to be an artefact of the later chronographers. The Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 abolished the consular tribunate and restored the consulship, with one place open to plebeians, alongside a new praetorship. The episode shows Roman institutional pragmatism: the Republic changed its top magistracy for seventy years without any formal constitution.

scholarship: Ridley, 'The consular tribunate: the testimony of Livy', Klio 68 (1986)

set.detail:
In 406, Livy reports, the Senate on its own initiative decreed that the soldiers should be paid from public funds, a measure greeted with joy by the plebs. To finance it a property tax (tributum) was levied on citizens according to their census rating; the senators led the way by paying first, and since there was as yet no coined money, they carried their bronze by weight to the treasury in wagons. The tribunes complained that the tax was a disguised burden on the poor. Diodorus also reports that during the Veientine war the Romans voted annual pay for their soldiers.

Pay made possible the long siege of Veii, including the first winter campaigns (Livy dates the first winter camp to 403). In the same years citizens of equestrian census without a public horse volunteered to serve on their own mounts, and cavalry pay was fixed. Livy also links the change from the round hoplite shield to the oblong scutum with the introduction of pay, a crucial step toward the manipular legion.

Tributum was not a regular annual tax but an extraordinary levy, sometimes treated as a forced loan to be repaid from booty, as happened after major victories; it was suspended entirely after 167 when the treasury filled with Macedonian wealth. Pay (stipendium, from stips, a small coin or bronze piece) remained modest, covering subsistence rather than providing a wage. Scholars have doubted that pay could exist before coinage, but payment in weighed bronze, or in grain and equipment, is plausible. Whatever the exact date, a state able to sustain armies beyond a summer season was a precondition of the conquest of Veii and of Rome's later expansion.
set.debate: Some scholars think pay before coinage is anachronistic, or that Livy has antedated a later practice; the nature and amount of early pay are unknown.

scholarship: Nicolet, The World of the Citizen in Republican Rome (1980) ch. 4

set.detail:
Veii stood on a tufa plateau of about 190 hectares, as large as Rome, 15 km north of it, controlling the right bank of the lower Tiber, the salt route from the coast and a territory (ager Veientanus) of some 560 km2. The two cities had fought intermittently for a century. The final war began in 406, and the tradition made the siege last ten years, like the siege of Troy. Its episodes mark real changes in Roman warfare: soldiers' pay from 406, winter camps from 403, volunteer cavalry, the loss of the siege lines in 402 through the quarrel of Sergius and Verginius, and the isolation of Veii when the Etruscan league refused help because the Veientes had chosen a king.

Religion frames the climax. In 398 the Alban Lake rose without rain; a captured Veientine haruspex and the Delphic oracle both declared that Veii would not fall until the water was drained, and the Romans cut the emissarium tunnel. In 396 M. Furius Camillus, named dictator with P. Cornelius Scipio as master of horse, had a tunnel dug under the walls to the citadel temple of Juno. Livy's anecdote has Roman soldiers emerging just as the Veientine king was sacrificing, and snatching the entrails so that Camillus could complete the sacrifice and claim its promise of victory. Camillus summoned Juno Regina to leave her city by evocatio; when a young soldier asked the statue if she wished to go to Rome, she nodded. The city was sacked, the free population sold, and Camillus triumphed in a chariot drawn by four white horses, offending the plebs by imitating Jupiter. A tenth of the booty was vowed to Apollo, and a gold bowl was sent to Delphi.

The conquest nearly doubled Roman territory. Four new tribes were created in 387, and plebeian proposals to move to Veii were narrowly defeated. Archaeology shows that Veii was not wiped out: sanctuaries such as Portonaccio and Campetti continued in use, and Roman settlers lived among the survivors. The network of drainage tunnels (cuniculi) around Veii may have inspired the tunnel story. For the first time Rome had destroyed a major Etruscan city and absorbed its land, the beginning of territorial conquest.

scholarship: Ward-Perkins, 'Veii: the historical topography of the ancient city', PBSR 29 (1961)

set.detail:
The disaster began at Clusium, which the Senonian Gauls were besieging. Three Fabian envoys sent by Rome to mediate broke the law of nations by fighting in the Clusine ranks, one of them killing a Gallic chieftain. When the Gauls demanded their surrender, the Roman people instead elected them consular tribunes for 390. The Gauls marched straight on Rome. The Roman army met them at the Allia, a stream that flows into the Tiber about 11 Roman miles north of the city on the Via Salaria. Livy says the commanders neglected the auspices and sacrifices, did not fortify a camp, and stretched the line thin to avoid being outflanked, placing reserves on a hill on the right. The Gallic leader Brennus attacked the reserves first; the main line broke at the war cry without fighting, and most of the fleeing soldiers swam the Tiber and took refuge in Veii, leaving Rome defenceless. Diodorus puts the battle on the right bank of the Tiber, which would explain the flight to Veii.

The date, 18 July, became the dies Alliensis, the blackest day in the Roman calendar, on which no public business was transacted. Polybius synchronised the capture of Rome with the Peace of Antalcidas and the siege of Rhegium by Dionysius, that is 387/386, which is why most modern scholars place the Allia about four years after the Varronian 390. Diodorus says the Romans had 24,000 men; Plutarch's 70,000 Gauls is a rhetorical figure.

The defeat was the worst in Roman memory before Cannae. Later tradition blamed religious failure and the Fabii's violation of the ius gentium, making the catastrophe a moral lesson. Militarily, the Gallic charge against a Roman phalanx in close order may have been one reason for the gradual adoption of a more flexible manipular line during the 4th century. The 'Gallic terror' (metus Gallicus) became a permanent theme of Roman policy, justifying the special treasury reserved for Gallic wars and the levies en masse (tumultus) of later centuries.

scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 715-722

set.detail:
Three days after the Allia (the day after, in some versions) the Gauls entered a city whose walls were undefended. The men of military age, the Senate and the treasures had gone up to the Capitol; the Flamen Quirinalis and the Vestals carried the sacred objects to Caere, helped by the plebeian L. Albinius. The aged ex-magistrates, says Livy, waited in their houses in their robes of office, sitting on ivory chairs; when a Gaul stroked the beard of M. Papirius, he struck him with his staff and was killed, and the massacre began. The city was plundered and burned. The Capitol held out. One night the Gauls climbed the cliff near the temple of Carmentis along a path found by following the Roman messenger Pontius Cominius, who had swum the Tiber to obtain the Senate's recall of Camillus from exile at Ardea. The sacred geese of Juno, spared despite the famine, woke M. Manlius, who threw the first Gaul down. After seven months, starving, the defenders agreed to pay 1,000 pounds of gold. When the Romans protested against false weights, Brennus threw his sword on the scale: 'vae victis', woe to the vanquished.

Livy has Camillus arrive as dictator at that moment, declare that Rome would be ransomed 'with iron, not gold', and destroy the Gauls. Other sources are less heroic. Polybius says the Gauls withdrew because the Veneti invaded their homeland and took the gold with them. Diodorus says the Caeretans ambushed them on the way home, and Strabo that Caere recovered the gold. Suetonius records that a Livius Drusus recovered the ransom in Gaul much later. The Gauls may have gone on south as mercenaries for Dionysius of Syracuse.

Archaeologically the sack left surprisingly little trace: the burnt layer in the Comitium once attributed to 390 is now dated to the 6th century. The trauma was nevertheless real. It produced the great wall of 378, a lasting fear of the Gauls, and the legend of Camillus as second founder. Greek writers of the 4th century, Heraclides Ponticus, Aristotle and Theopompus, knew of the capture, the first Roman event to enter Greek literature.

scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 719-747

set.detail:
Livy's terse notice under 378, that the censors let a contract for a wall 'of squared stone', is confirmed by the surviving stretches of the so-called Servian Wall, built of large blocks of yellowish Grotta Oscura tufa quarried in the territory of Veii, which Rome controlled only after 396. The wall ran for about 11 km and enclosed some 426 hectares, including all seven hills, the largest walled area of any Italian city of the time and comparable only to the Dionysian circuit of Syracuse. Where the plateau of the Esquiline, Viminal and Quirinal offered no natural defence, it took the form of an agger, a massive earth rampart faced with stone, fronted by a ditch about 30 m wide and up to 17 m deep. Blocks bear masons' marks in Greek letters, suggesting Greek contractors or workmen, perhaps from Syracuse or Magna Graecia.

Roman tradition attributed the city wall to King Servius Tullius, and remains of an earlier fortification in local cappellaccio tufa, probably of the 6th century, have been found beneath parts of the later circuit, so the 378 wall may have rebuilt and enlarged an archaic line. The best-preserved sections today are outside Termini station and on the Aventine in Via di Sant'Anselmo, where an arch for a catapult belongs to repairs of the early 1st century BC. Gates included the Porta Capena (start of the Via Appia), Collina, Esquilina, Viminalis, Caelimontana and Trigemina.

The wall answered the trauma of 390: never again would the city be open to raiders. It was repaired in 353, during the Second Punic War, when Hannibal reached the Anio in 211 and did not attempt an assault, and in the civil wars of the 80s. As the city outgrew it under the late Republic and Augustus it lost its function, and Rome remained unwalled until Aurelian's wall of 271-275.
set.debate: Whether the 378 wall replaced an earlier 6th-century circuit, and the precise extent of the original enclosure, are debated; the Grotta Oscura tufa gives a terminus post quem of 396.

scholarship: Säflund, Le mura di Roma repubblicana (1932)
Cifani, 'The fortifications of archaic Rome', in Frederiksen et al. (eds), Focus on Fortifications (2016)

set.detail:
From 376 the tribunes C. Licinius Stolo and L. Sextius Lateranus proposed three bills together: that interest already paid be deducted from the principal of debts and the remainder repaid in three annual instalments; that no one should possess more than 500 iugera (about 125 ha) of public land; and that the consular tribunate be abolished and one consul be plebeian. According to Livy they were re-elected tribunes ten times, used their veto to prevent elections of curule magistrates for five years (the 'anarchy' of 375-371, now thought to be a chronological fiction), and finally, in 367, carried the laws against patrician resistance led by the aged Camillus, named dictator for the last time. A further law replaced the patrician duoviri sacris faciundis, keepers of the Sibylline Books, with a board of ten, half plebeian.

The compromise of 367 created two new patrician offices to compensate: a praetor with imperium for jurisdiction, and two curule aediles to manage the city and the Roman Games, which were extended by a day. Sextius became the first plebeian consul in 366, L. Genucius the second in 365. Camillus vowed a temple of Concord to celebrate reconciliation, though this tradition may be later invention. The law did not ensure a plebeian consul every year: patrician pairs appear in 355, 353, 351, 349, 345 and 343, until the lex Genucia of 342 made the arrangement permanent and even allowed both consuls to be plebeian.

The laws are the turning point of the Struggle of the Orders. They opened the consulship, and so the Senate, to wealthy plebeian families, creating the patricio-plebeian nobility (nobilitas) that dominated Rome for three centuries. The land clause is the most debated: many think the 500-iugera limit a retrojection of the Gracchan law of 133, which reaffirmed it, but Cato's speech for the Rhodians in 167 mentions a law forbidding the possession of more than 500 iugera, showing that some such rule existed by then. Livy records that Licinius himself was fined 10,000 asses under his own law in 357 for holding 1,000 iugera through his emancipated son.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, I (1997) 645-661

set.detail:
When the Latins demanded, through their spokesman L. Annius of Setia, that one consul and half the Senate be Latin, the Romans refused and war followed. The consuls T. Manlius Torquatus and P. Decius Mus marched, according to Livy, through the land of the Marsi and Paeligni to join the Samnites and confronted the Latin and Campanian army near Mount Vesuvius on the road to Veseris. Before the battle Manlius' son, provoked by the Tusculan cavalry commander Geminus Maecius, fought him against orders and killed him; his father had him executed before the army, and 'Manlian commands' became a proverb for pitiless discipline. Both consuls dreamed that the general on one side and the army on the other were owed to the gods of the underworld.

In the battle the Roman left, under Decius, began to give way. Decius called the pontifex M. Valerius, who dictated the formula of devotio: veiled, his toga girt in the Gabine manner, standing on a spear, Decius invoked Janus, Jupiter, Mars, Quirinus, Bellona, the Lares, the Novensiles and Indigetes, and the Di Manes, devoting himself and the legions and auxiliaries of the enemy to the gods below. He then rode into the Latin ranks and was killed, and his body was found next day under a heap of enemy dead. Manlius held his triarii in reserve until the Latins were exhausted, then threw them in; Livy says scarcely a quarter of the enemy escaped. The victory at Trifanum soon after completed the campaign.

Livy uses the battle for his set-piece description of the manipular legion with hastati, principes and triarii, a passage historians treat as partly anachronistic. The devotio formula is precious evidence of archaic religion, whatever its historicity. Cicero knew of three Decii who devoted themselves (340, 295 and 279); some scholars think the first is a doublet of the second, better attested by the contemporary Greek Duris. The location is uncertain, since a march through the Abruzzi would bring the consuls toward northern Campania, and 'Veseris' has been sought near Vescia and Suessa rather than the volcano.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, II (1998) 477-487
Versnel, 'Two types of Roman devotio', Mnemosyne 29 (1976)

set.detail:
After victories at Pedum and the Astura in 338, the consuls L. Furius Camillus and C. Maenius asked the Senate how to deal with Latium. The resulting settlement, preserved by Livy, treated each community separately and is the foundation of the Roman system of Italy. Lanuvium received full citizenship, its temple of Juno Sospita being shared with the Roman people; Aricia, Nomentum and Pedum received citizenship on the same terms as Lanuvium; Tusculum kept the citizenship granted in 381, its leaders of the revolt being punished. Velitrae, an old Roman colony that had revolted repeatedly, had its walls razed, its senate deported across the Tiber (any senator caught on the near side to be fined 1,000 asses) and its land given to new settlers. Antium received a colony, its warships were burned or taken to Rome's dockyards, their beaks adorned the Rostra, and its people were forbidden the sea. Tibur and Praeneste lost land but remained allies with their own treaties. The other Latin cities lost conubium, commercium and the right of assembly with each other, keeping those rights only with Rome. The Campanian cavalry were rewarded with citizenship, while Capua, Fundi, Formiae, Cumae and Suessula received citizenship without the vote (civitas sine suffragio).

The settlement created graded statuses that defined Roman Italy. Full citizen communities later became municipia; communities with citizenship without the vote shared the obligations (munera) of citizens, above all military service, while governing themselves; Latin communities, old and new, kept the Latin rights of the Foedus Cassianum; and the Latin status became transferable, so that new colonies such as Cales (334) were founded as Latin cities. Two new tribes, the Maecia and Scaptia, were added in 332. Roman territory grew to about 5,500 km2 and the citizen body to perhaps 350,000-400,000 people.

Modern historians see 338 as the moment Rome ceased to be a city-state leading a league and became the centre of a territorial state with a network of dependent allies. The divide-and-rule logic, combining generosity and severity, was applied to every later conquest in Italy, and the manpower it generated allowed Rome to absorb defeats like the Caudine Forks, Heraclea and Cannae.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, II (1998) 538-571

set.detail:
Nexum was a contract by bronze and scales (per aes et libram) by which a borrower pledged his own person and labour as security, becoming a bondsman (nexus) of his creditor until the debt was paid. Livy's story for 326 tells of a young man, C. Publilius, who had entered bondage to the moneylender L. Papirius for his father's debt. Papirius, attracted by his youth, tried first persuasion and then threats; when the young man resisted, he had him stripped and flogged. Publilius ran into the street showing the welts; a crowd gathered, the consuls were forced to convene the Senate, and a law was carried that no one should be kept in fetters or chains except those guilty of crime awaiting punishment, and that for money lent, the debtor's goods, not his body, should be liable. All nexi were released. Livy calls it 'as it were a second beginning of liberty' for the plebs. Dionysius tells a similar story with different names, and Varro dates the law to the dictatorship of C. Poetelius Libo Visolus in 313.

The law did not end all debt bondage: judgment debtors (addicti) could still be handed over to creditors to work off debts, a practice attested into the late Republic. What it ended was the voluntary self-pledge of citizens as a normal credit mechanism. Moses Finley argued that this was a turning point in Roman social history: once citizens could no longer be exploited as bonded labour, Roman landowners turned to chattel slaves imported through war, and the great slave society of the later Republic followed. The wars of the late 4th century supplied captives in quantity, from the 4,000 Satricans sold in 346 to the tens of thousands of Samnites enslaved in the 290s.

The law also strengthened the free peasantry as the backbone of the legions. Its anecdotal origin, a sexual assault on a free citizen's body like the Verginia story, expresses the Roman idea that libertas meant the inviolability of the citizen's person.
set.debate: Date (326 Livy, 313 Varro) and the scope of the abolition are disputed; debt bondage by judgment survived.

scholarship: Finley, 'Debt-bondage and the problem of slavery', in Economy and Society in Ancient Greece (1981)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, II (1998) 688-700

set.detail:
In 321 the consuls T. Veturius Calvinus and Sp. Postumius Albinus were camped with four legions near Calatia in Campania when ten Samnite soldiers disguised as shepherds, posted by the Samnite general Gavius Pontius, told Roman foragers that the Samnite army was besieging Luceria in Apulia. Eager to relieve their ally, the consuls took the shortest route, through the Caudine pass. Livy describes the trap precisely: a grassy, enclosed plain between wooded ridges, entered and left by narrow defiles. The Romans passed through the first, found the exit blocked by felled trees and boulders, turned back and found the entrance blocked too, with Samnites on the heights. They fortified a camp and waited in vain.

Pontius consulted his aged father Herennius, who advised releasing the Romans unharmed to win their friendship, or else killing them all to cripple Rome for a generation; anything between, he warned, would earn hatred without weakening them. Pontius chose the middle course. The terms: the Romans would evacuate Samnite territory, withdraw their colonies at Cales and Fregellae, and restore the old treaty; 600 equites were given as hostages; and the whole army, consuls included, passed under a 'yoke' of spears, stripped to their tunics. Capua received the shamed soldiers kindly; they entered Rome by night.

The disaster cost no lives but enormous prestige. Livy insists the agreement was only a sponsio, a personal pledge by the commanders, not a treaty sworn by fetials, and makes the Romans repudiate it in 320, handing over Postumius and the other guarantors, whom Pontius refused, and avenging themselves at Luceria. Modern scholars mostly believe Rome honoured the peace for some years, as Cicero and Appian imply, until the war resumed in 316 or 315. The location is traditionally the valley between Arpaia and Montesarchio (the Forchia di Arpaia preserving the name 'furculae'), though Salmon and others preferred the valley of Moiano. The Caudine Forks became shorthand for humiliation; passing 'under the Caudine yoke' is still an Italian idiom.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, III (2005) 1-21

set.detail:
As censor in 312 Appius Claudius Caecus built, without waiting for Senate approval and draining the treasury, the road that bears his name, the first Roman highway named after its builder. It ran 132 Roman miles from the Porta Capena to Capua: through Bovillae and Aricia, across the Alban hills, then in a long straight line across the Pontine marshes to Tarracina, along the coast past Fundi and Formiae to Minturnae and Sinuessa, and inland to Capua. The 19-mile stretch through the marshes (the decennovium) ran beside a canal; Horace describes taking the night barge from Forum Appii to the shrine of Feronia near Tarracina, tormented by frogs and mosquitoes. At first the road was surfaced with gravel; in 296 the curule aediles laid a stone footpath from the Porta Capena to the temple of Mars, in 293 the road was paved with silex from there to Bovillae, and the familiar polygonal blocks of basalt gradually extended along the route.

The strategic logic is clear. The older route to Campania, the Via Latina, ran up the Sacco and Liris valleys through country exposed to Samnite attack; after Lautulae (315) Rome needed a secure coastal corridor to its Campanian allies, linking the colonies of Tarracina (329), Suessa (313), Minturnae and Sinuessa (296). The road was extended to Beneventum after 268, then to Venusia and Tarentum, and by the early 2nd century to Brundisium, the port for the East.

Ancient writers admired it as the 'queen of roads' (Statius). Procopius, travelling it 800 years after its construction, marvelled that the stones were fitted so tightly without mortar that they seemed to have grown together, and that it took five days for a traveller to cover it. Along its first miles outside Rome the aristocracy built its tombs, including the tomb of the Scipios, begun in the early 3rd century. Diodorus' claim that Appius paved most of it in stone in 312 is generally thought anachronistic, and some scholars think the censor improved an existing track rather than building a new road.
set.debate: Whether the whole route was built new in 312 and when it was paved; Diodorus' account of stone paving in 312 is probably anachronistic.

scholarship: Laurence, The Roads of Roman Italy (1999)

set.detail:
In 296 the Samnite general Gellius Egnatius led an army north to join the Etruscans, Umbrians and Senonian Gauls in a coalition against Rome. Rome answered with an unprecedented effort: both consuls, Q. Fabius Rullianus (for the fifth time) and P. Decius Mus (for the fourth), marched with four legions and as many allies, while two propraetors, Cn. Fulvius and L. Postumius Megellus, ravaged the territory of Clusium to draw the Etruscans and Umbrians home. The Romans met the Samnites and Gauls in 295 at Sentinum, near modern Sassoferrato, on the Umbrian side of the Apennines.

Before the battle a hind chased by a wolf ran between the lines; the hind fled to the Gauls and was killed, the wolf, sacred to Mars, passed through the Roman ranks unharmed, an omen Livy reports. Fabius, on the right against the Samnites, held back to tire them; Decius, on the left against the Gauls, charged with his cavalry and was thrown back by Gallic war chariots, a weapon the Romans had not met, which terrified the horses. As his line broke, Decius summoned the pontifex M. Livius, recited the formula of devotio his father had used in 340, and rode to his death. The left steadied; Fabius sent reserves, then used the Campanian cavalry to take the Samnites in flank and rear, and stormed their camp. Gellius Egnatius was killed. Livy gives 25,000 enemy dead and 8,000 prisoners, Roman losses of 8,700 (7,000 in Decius' army). The Greek historian Duris of Samos, nearly contemporary, gives 100,000 enemy dead, a figure that shows how the battle impressed the Greek world.

Sentinum was the largest battle yet fought in Italy and decided its future. It broke the only coalition that might have contained Rome; the Etruscans and Umbrians soon sought truces, the Gauls were left isolated, and the Samnites fought on alone until 290. Fabius vowed a temple to Jupiter Victor; the curule aediles Ogulnii set up the bronze she-wolf with the twins in the same year. Polybius mentions the battle briefly in his account of the Gallic wars, which confirms its reality against those who doubt the annalistic details.
set.debate: Ancient casualty figures conflict (Livy 25,000 enemy dead, Duris 100,000); whether Etruscans and Umbrians fought, and the historicity of the second Decian devotio, are debated.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, IV (2005) 277-345

set.detail:
After the Samnite and Sabine wars a debt crisis led the plebs, in 287, to secede for the last time, to the Janiculum. Livy's account is lost, and only the summary of book 11 survives: 'the plebs seceded to the Janiculum because of debt after serious and long seditions; it was brought back by the dictator Q. Hortensius, who died in office'. Hortensius, a plebeian, carried a law that resolutions of the plebeian assembly (plebiscita) should bind all citizens (ut quod plebs iussisset omnes Quirites teneret). Gaius and the jurist Laelius Felix, quoted by Gellius, record that the patricians had previously claimed not to be bound by plebiscites. Macrobius adds that a lex Hortensia made market days (nundinae) days on which legal business could be done, so that country people coming to town could settle their lawsuits.

The law has a puzzling history, since the same principle is credited to the Valerio-Horatian laws of 449 and the Publilian law of 339. The usual solution is that the earlier laws required the patrician senators' approval (auctoritas patrum) for plebiscites, and that Hortensius removed this condition, making the plebeian council a fully sovereign legislature. In the same secession, according to Byzantine tradition, the lex Aquilia on wrongful damage was passed.

Modern historians treat 287 as the formal end of the Struggle of the Orders. From then on most legislation was passed as plebiscites proposed by tribunes in the concilium plebis, and the tribunes, now drawn from the same noble families as the consuls, became instruments of senatorial government. The integration lasted until Tiberius Gracchus in 133 rediscovered the tribunate's revolutionary potential. The law also illustrates a paradox of the Roman constitution: the plebeian assembly, technically a meeting of part of the people, became the main legislature of the whole.
set.debate: Relationship to the laws of 449 and 339; the cause of the crisis (debt) is known only from the Periochae and Zonaras.

scholarship: Hölkeskamp, 'The Roman Republic: government of the people, by the people, for the people?', SCI 19 (2000)

set.detail:
Tarentum, the richest Greek city of Italy, had long regarded the Gulf of Tarentum as its own water. A treaty, mentioned by Appian, forbade Roman warships to sail east of the Lacinian promontory near Croton; its date is uncertain, often put around 303 when Cleonymus campaigned in Italy. By 282 Rome had placed garrisons in Thurii and other Greek cities appealing for protection against the Lucanians, cities Tarentum considered its sphere. In that year a squadron of ten Roman ships, commanded by a duumvir whom Appian calls L. Cornelius and Dio L. Valerius, sailed into the gulf, perhaps on the way to the Adriatic, and appeared off Tarentum. The Tarentines, gathered in their theatre overlooking the harbour for the festival of Dionysus, were stirred by the demagogue Philocharis to attack; four ships were sunk, one captured with its crew, and the commander killed. The Tarentines then marched on Thurii, expelled the Roman garrison and plundered the city.

Rome sent an embassy led by L. Postumius Megellus to demand redress. The Tarentines laughed at his Greek and at the purple-bordered toga, and a drunken man named Philonides fouled the toga in front of the assembly. Postumius, holding up the stained garment, told them to laugh while they could: they would weep long, when it was washed clean with their blood. The Senate debated; the war party prevailed, and in 281 the consul L. Aemilius Barbula invaded Tarentine territory. Tarentum, unable to face Rome alone, sent for Pyrrhus of Epirus.

The anecdotes come from Dionysius, Appian and Dio, all writing under the influence of Roman tradition, which portrayed the Tarentines as frivolous and insolent. Modern historians debate whether the Roman squadron's appearance was innocent or a deliberate breach of the treaty to test Tarentine resolve, and whether the treaty itself existed in the form described. Either way the incident shows how Rome's acceptance of appeals from Greek cities in the south led to collision with Tarentum, just as its acceptance of the Mamertine appeal would lead to war with Carthage.
set.debate: Whether the Roman squadron deliberately violated the Lacinian treaty, the treaty's date and the identity of the Roman commander are all disputed.

set.detail:
Pyrrhus landed at Tarentum in 280 after a storm scattered his fleet; Plutarch says he brought 20,000 infantry, 3,000 cavalry, 2,000 archers, 500 slingers and 20 elephants, of which not all arrived. He imposed military discipline on the Tarentines, closing their gymnasia and theatres. The consul P. Valerius Laevinus marched into Lucania to prevent the Samnites and Lucanians from joining the king, and the armies met on the plain between Heraclea and Pandosia, divided by the river Siris. Inspecting the Roman camp, Pyrrhus is said to have remarked that the order of these barbarians was not barbarian.

The Romans crossed the Siris, their cavalry fording upstream to outflank the Epirote position. Pyrrhus led his own cavalry, was nearly killed when his horse was struck down, and exchanged armour with his companion Megacles, whose death in the king's cloak and helmet caused panic until Pyrrhus showed himself bareheaded. The phalanx and the legions advanced and gave way seven times. Pyrrhus then sent in the elephants, which the Romans had never seen; the horses bolted, and the Thessalian cavalry completed the rout. A Roman soldier, C. Minucius of the fourth legion's hastati, is said to have wounded an elephant and caused disorder. The Romans fled back across the river; their camp was taken.

Losses are disputed. Dionysius gives 15,000 Romans and 13,000 of Pyrrhus' men, while Hieronymus of Cardia, who used the king's own memoirs, gives 7,000 Romans and just under 4,000 Pyrrhic dead, including many of the king's best officers. The victory brought the Lucanians, Samnites and Greek cities such as Locri and Croton over to Pyrrhus, and the Campanian garrison seized Rhegium. Pyrrhus advanced on Rome, reaching Anagnia or Praeneste, but Rome refused to negotiate. The battle introduced Rome to Hellenistic warfare and to elephants, the 'Lucanian oxen', and demonstrated that a beaten Roman army could be replaced almost at once.
set.debate: Casualty figures conflict (Hieronymus 7,000 Romans and under 4,000 Pyrrhic dead; Dionysius 15,000 and 13,000); the size of both armies is uncertain.

set.detail:
After his march on Rome failed and Cineas' peace mission was rebuffed, Pyrrhus campaigned in Apulia in 279. The consuls P. Sulpicius Saverrio and P. Decius Mus met him near Ausculum (Ascoli Satriano), by a river later identified with the Carapelle. Dionysius gives a detailed order of battle: each side about 70,000 infantry and 8,000 cavalry, Pyrrhus with 19 elephants and his Macedonian and Epirote phalanx interspersed with Italian allies, a sensible reconstruction even if the numbers are inflated. The Romans had prepared 300 ox-drawn wagons armed with spikes, scythes and fire-pots to counter the elephants.

The first day was fought on rough, wooded ground near the river where the phalanx and the elephants could not operate freely, and ended inconclusively. On the second day Pyrrhus occupied the broken ground with light troops and forced the battle onto the plain. The legions fought the phalanx hard, the anti-elephant wagons were overwhelmed by the light troops escorting the elephants, and the elephants drove back the Roman line; the Romans retreated to their camp. Pyrrhus was wounded in the arm by a javelin. Meanwhile his Daunian allies plundered his own camp. Plutarch, using Hieronymus, gives 6,000 Roman dead and 3,505 on Pyrrhus' side according to the royal records, and records the king's remark, when congratulated, that one more such victory would ruin him, the origin of the phrase 'Pyrrhic victory'.

Roman tradition claimed a draw or even a victory, and Cicero believed that the third Decius devoted himself at Ausculum like his father and grandfather; Zonaras says Pyrrhus warned the Romans he would take alive anyone attempting the rite, and the story may be invented. Strategically the battle was decisive in the opposite direction: Pyrrhus could not replace his Epirote veterans, Rome replaced its losses, and the king turned to the invitation from the Sicilian Greeks against Carthage, leaving Italy for three years.

Pyrrhus returned from Sicily in 276 with a weakened army, having lost many ships in a sea battle with the Carthaginians in the Strait and fought off a Mamertine ambush near Rhegium; he plundered the treasury of Persephone at Locri to pay his men. In 275 the consul M'. Curius Dentatus was in Samnium near Maleventum, his colleague L. Cornelius Lentulus in Lucania. Pyrrhus detached a force to hold Lentulus and marched against Curius before the two could unite, planning to surprise his camp by a night march through wooded hills. The march went wrong: the torches burned out, the troops lost their way, and at dawn they arrived on the heights above the Roman camp, exhausted and in full view.

Curius led his men out, attacked the van and routed it, capturing some elephants. In the main battle on the plain the elephants drove the Romans back toward their camp, where reserves or camp guards attacked them with missiles; according to Florus, Orosius and Zonaras, a wounded elephant calf screamed, its mother rampaged through the Epirote lines, and the other elephants panicked. Pyrrhus withdrew to Tarentum and soon sailed for Epirus with 8,000 infantry and 500 cavalry, leaving a garrison under Milo. Curius' triumph displayed four captured elephants, the first seen in Rome.

The scale of the battle is unclear. Orosius' figures (80,000 Pyrrhic troops, 33,000 killed) are absurd, and Plutarch's account suggests a sharp defeat rather than annihilation. Some modern historians, like Lévêque, consider it a limited reverse and argue that Pyrrhus left because of shortage of money and the opportunity in Macedonia, where Antigonus Gonatas was vulnerable. The site is also disputed: Florus places it 'in Lucania, on the Arusine plains', while Plutarch and others place it at Maleventum. Rome renamed Maleventum, 'ill-come', as Beneventum, 'well-come', when it founded a Latin colony there in 268, a sign of how the battle was remembered.
set.debate: Location (Maleventum or the Arusine plains) and the decisiveness of the battle are debated; ancient casualty figures are unreliable.

When Pyrrhus left Italy in 275 he kept a garrison under his general Milo in the citadel of Tarentum, with his son Helenus. After the king's death in a street fight at Argos in 272, Helenus was recalled, and the consuls L. Papirius Cursor and Sp. Carvilius closed in on Tarentum, where pro-Roman and anti-Roman factions were fighting. A Carthaginian fleet appeared off the harbour, ostensibly to help the Tarentines; the Romans later cited it as a breach of the treaty of 279, and Carthage denied any hostile intent. Milo negotiated the surrender of the citadel to Papirius in return for safe passage for himself and his troops.

Tarentum surrendered its arms and fleet, its walls were demolished according to Zonaras, a Roman garrison occupied the acropolis, and the city became an allied state (socius navalis) obliged to supply ships rather than soldiers. Papirius triumphed over the Tarentines and Carvilius over the Samnites, Lucanians and Bruttii, completing the reduction of the south. The booty, including works of Greek art, enriched Rome; Papirius used his share for the temple of Consus. Among the captives was a young Greek, Andronicus, who became the slave and then freedman of a Livius and, as Livius Andronicus, translated the Odyssey into Latin and staged the first Latin plays in 240.

The fall of Tarentum, with the last resistance of the Samnites and the Bruttii in 272, left Rome master of the peninsula south of a line from Pisa to Ariminum, an alliance of perhaps 3 million people bound by treaties and colonies. Within eight years Rome crossed the Strait to Sicily. The Carthaginian fleet's appearance at Tarentum foreshadowed that conflict: each power now regarded the other with suspicion, and Polybius' treaty sequence breaks off with the alliance of 279.
set.debate: The Carthaginian fleet's intentions and whether Tarentum's walls were really demolished are uncertain.
