Lucius Tarquinius, called Superbus ('the Proud'), was by tradition the seventh and last king of Rome (534-509), son or grandson of Tarquinius Priscus. He came to power through crime: married to Tullia, daughter of King Servius Tullius, after each had murdered their first spouses, he seized the throne, had Servius killed in the street, and Tullia drove her carriage over her father's body in the street thereafter called the Vicus Sceleratus. He ruled without consulting the Senate, executed his opponents, and forced the plebs to labour on the Capitoline temple and the Cloaca Maxima.

He was also the most powerful of the kings. He presided over the Latin council at the spring of Ferentina and had its rebellious spokesman Turnus Herdonius of Aricia drowned; he took Suessa Pometia, captured Gabii through his son Sextus' treachery (signalling with the famous lopping of the tallest poppies, a motif borrowed from Herodotus' story of Thrasybulus and Periander), concluded the treaty with Gabii kept in the temple of Dius Fidius, and planted colonies at Signia and Circeii. Legend made him buy the Sibylline Books from an old woman who burned six of the nine before he paid her full price for the last three. The first treaty with Carthage, which assumes Roman hegemony over the coastal Latin cities, reflects his dominion.

Expelled in 509 after his son's rape of Lucretia, he spent fourteen years trying to return, with Veii and Tarquinii at the Silva Arsia, with Porsenna, and with the Latins at Lake Regillus, before dying in exile at Cumae in 495, the guest of the tyrant Aristodemus. Modern historians see the Superbus portrait as a Greek tyrant stereotype grafted on to a real ruler, possibly of the Etruscan Tarchna family; the archaeology of late 6th-century Rome, a city of some 285 hectares with monumental temples and drains, fits a strong monarchy. The François Tomb at Vulci, showing the killing of a 'Cneve Tarchunies Rumach', preserves an Etruscan memory of the Tarquins in internecine wars.

L. Junius Brutus was, according to tradition, the son of Tarquinius Superbus' sister, who survived his uncle's murder of his father and brother by pretending to be dim-witted, earning the name brutus ('dullard'). Sent to Delphi with the king's sons, he carried a gold rod hidden in a hollow staff as his offering, and when the oracle said the first to kiss his mother would rule Rome, he pretended to stumble and kissed the earth, mother of all. When Lucretia killed herself he drew the knife from her body and swore the oath that began the revolution, harangued the people in the Forum, won over the army at Ardea, and was elected consul with Collatinus in 509.

As consul he made the people swear never to allow a king, enlarged the Senate to 300 by enrolling equestrian leaders (conscripti), and persuaded Collatinus to resign. He presided over the trial of the royalist conspirators, among them his own sons Titus and Tiberius, and watched unmoved as they were scourged and beheaded. In the battle at the Silva Arsia against Veii and Tarquinii, Brutus and Arruns, son of Tarquin, charged each other and fell together; the matrons mourned him for a year as the avenger of chastity. A bronze statue of him with drawn sword stood on the Capitol among the statues of the kings.

Brutus is the founding hero of Republican liberty, but his historicity is doubtful. The plebeian Junii Bruti of the later Republic claimed descent from him, which the tradition that he executed his only sons made awkward; Posidonius invented a third son to save the claim. His most famous descendant, M. Junius Brutus, put the first consul's head on his coins (54 BC, with the legend BRVTVS and the image of Servilius Ahala) and was urged by anonymous graffiti at the statue on the Capitol to live up to his ancestor before the Ides of March 44.

P. Valerius, later called Publicola or Poplicola ('friend of the people'), belonged to a gens said to descend from the Sabine Volesus who came to Rome with Titus Tatius. He was one of the witnesses of Lucretia's death and the oath, was elected suffect consul after Collatinus' resignation in 509, and was consul again in 508, 507 and 504 by the traditional count. After Brutus' death he governed alone for a time, and suspicion that he aimed at kingship was dispelled by his demolition of his house on the Velia and by lowering the fasces before the people.

A cluster of measures is credited to him: the first law granting citizens a right of appeal (provocatio) against capital sentences by magistrates, a law making anyone who aspired to kingship sacer, so that he could be killed without trial, the appointment of quaestors to administer the treasury in the temple of Saturn, and a rule that magistrates' fasces carry no axes in the city. He triumphed over Veii after the Silva Arsia, fought Porsenna, and in 504 celebrated a triumph over the Sabines in the year Attus Clausus migrated to Rome. He died in 503 so poor that the state paid for his funeral, the women mourned him for a year, and his family received the right of burial inside the city.

Plutarch paired Publicola's Life with that of Solon, as the lawgiver of a free state. Modern scholars attribute much of his image to the Valerian family tradition, transmitted by the 1st-century annalist Valerius Antias, who credited Valerii with every popular law (509, 449, 300). The Lapis Satricanus, a dedication of c. 500 to Mars by the 'companions of Poplios Valesios', has been tentatively linked to him, though the identification is disputed. If accepted, it shows a Valerius leading a private war band, a world of aristocratic warlords far from the civic hero of tradition.

Lars Porsenna (Lars is an Etruscan praenomen or title; the name may render Etruscan Purthna) was king of Clusium, the inland Etruscan city on the Chiana valley route from Etruria to Latium. Roman tradition says he besieged Rome in 508 to restore Tarquinius Superbus, occupied the Janiculum, and blockaded the city until the heroism of Horatius Cocles, Mucius Scaevola and Cloelia convinced him to make peace, receiving hostages and the return of the Veientine land. He then sent his son Arruns against Aricia, where the Latins and Aristodemus of Cumae defeated and killed him in 504, and returned the hostages, after which Rome gave him an ivory throne, sceptre, golden crown and triumphal robe.

The other evidence suggests he took Rome. Tacitus speaks of the city's surrender (dedita urbe) to Porsenna; Pliny quotes the treaty forbidding the Romans the use of iron except for farming; and the gifts sent to him are insignia of submission. He may have expelled Tarquin himself, as some modern historians suggest, before his power in Latium collapsed after Aricia. The surviving Etruscan fugitives were settled at Rome in the Vicus Tuscus, and Roman auctions kept a ritual phrase, 'the goods of King Porsenna are for sale'.

Etruscan memory made him a figure of legend. Varro, quoted by Pliny, describes his tomb at Clusium as a square base 300 feet each side containing an inextricable labyrinth, crowned by five pyramids and a bronze disc hung with bells, and above that further tiers of pyramids. Pliny called the description 'fabulous'. Attempts to identify the tomb in the tunnels under Chiusi or at the Poggio Gaiella tumulus have not succeeded. Pliny also reports that Porsenna called down lightning to kill a monster, a sign of the Etruscan reputation for controlling heavenly signs.

Cn. Marcius Coriolanus is the most famous early Roman whose existence is doubtful. According to Livy, Dionysius and Plutarch, he was a young patrician of the Marcian gens, raised by his widowed mother, who won a civic crown at Lake Regillus and in 493, as a junior officer, captured the Volscian town of Corioli almost single-handed, earning his cognomen. Proud and contemptuous of the plebs, he proposed during the famine of 491 that the grain sent from Sicily be withheld unless the plebs gave up the tribunate. Summoned to trial by the tribunes, he refused to appear, was condemned in absence, and went into exile to the Volscian leader Attius Tullius at Antium.

In 488 he led a Volscian army against Rome, taking Circeii, Satricum, Longula, Polusca, Corioli, Lavinium and other Latin towns, and camped at the Fossae Cluiliae, five miles from the city. He sent back delegations of senators and of priests in their robes. Only when his mother Veturia, his wife Volumnia and their children came at the head of the Roman matrons did he yield, saying (in Livy's version) that his mother had saved Rome and ruined her son. The temple of Fortuna Muliebris marked the spot. His end is uncertain: Dionysius and Plutarch say the Volsci killed him as a traitor; Livy reports Fabius Pictor's version that he lived to old age in exile, lamenting that exile is bitterer for an old man.

Modern scholars note that no Marcius appears in the early Fasti and that cognomina derived from conquered towns are otherwise later. The story may combine a genuine memory of Volscian advances into Latium in the 480s, possibly under a Latin or Roman renegade, with a moral tale about pride, family and the limits of personal glory. Plutarch paired him with Alcibiades, and Shakespeare's tragedy (c. 1608), based on North's Plutarch, made him a lasting figure of political drama.

Sp. Cassius Vecellinus was the dominant statesman of the first generation of the Republic. Tradition makes him consul three times: in 502, when he triumphed over the Sabines; in 493, when he concluded the treaty with the Latins that bears his name and dedicated the temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera; and in 486, when he made a treaty with the Hernici admitting them to the Latin alliance. He is also listed as the first master of horse, under the dictator T. Larcius in 501.

In his third consulship he proposed the first agrarian law, distributing land taken from the Hernici and public land occupied by patricians among the plebs and the Latins. His colleague Proculus Verginius and the Senate opposed him, accusing him of buying popularity to make himself king. In 485, after his term, he was condemned and executed. Livy gives two versions: that his own father tried him in a domestic court and had him scourged and killed, dedicating his property to Ceres in a statue inscribed 'given from the Cassian family'; or that the quaestors Caeso Fabius and L. Valerius accused him before the people, who condemned him. His house was razed, and the site, an open space before the later temple of Tellus, remained a warning.

Cassius is the first of the three men of the early Republic, with Sp. Maelius (439) and M. Manlius Capitolinus (384), killed for 'aiming at kingship' (adfectatio regni), a charge that late Republican writers used against the Gracchi and others. His agrarian law is widely seen as a retrojection of Gracchan controversies. But his career is plausible in outline, and his treaties are well attested: Cicero saw the text of the Foedus Cassianum on a bronze column. The later Cassii, including Caesar's assassin, were plebeian, and later writers struggled to connect them with him.

L. Quinctius Cincinnatus ('the curly-haired') is the archetype of the citizen-farmer called to save the state. A patrician of an established family, he was impoverished after his son Caeso jumped bail in 461 and the sureties' pledges had to be paid; he retired to a farm of four iugera across the Tiber, later called the Prata Quinctia. In 460, after the consul P. Valerius fell retaking the Capitol from Appius Herdonius, he was elected suffect consul and spoke harshly against the tribunes.

In 458 the Aequi under Gracchus Cloelius trapped the consul L. Minucius and his army on Mount Algidus. Envoys of the Senate found Cincinnatus ploughing, or digging a ditch, and asked him to put on his toga to hear their message; his wife Racilia fetched it from the cottage, and he was hailed as dictator. He chose L. Tarquitius as master of horse, closed the courts, ordered every man of military age to report with five days' food and twelve stakes, marched by night, and enclosed the Aequi with a ditch and palisade. Caught between two Roman armies, they surrendered and passed under the yoke. Cincinnatus triumphed and laid down the dictatorship after sixteen days. In 439, aged about eighty, he was named dictator again to deal with Sp. Maelius, whom his master of horse C. Servilius Ahala killed in the Forum.

The details are legendary, and the four-iugera farm sits oddly with a wealthy patrician house; the episode may also be a doublet of other rescues of trapped armies. But its moral power proved enormous. Livy uses it to show contempt for wealth in early Rome, and it became a model for Republican virtue in the modern world: George Washington was hailed as the American Cincinnatus when he resigned his command in 1783, officers of the Continental Army founded the Society of the Cincinnati, and the city of Cincinnati in Ohio was named after it.

Ap. Claudius, called Crassus Inregillensis Sabinus in the Fasti, probably a son or grandson of Attus Clausus, was consul-designate for 451 when the consulship was suspended and the first board of decemvirs was elected to write the laws. He was its leading member and, in Livy's narrative, a skilled populist who courted the plebs. When a second board was elected for 450, he manipulated the elections to secure his own re-election alongside compliant colleagues, including men of plebeian names, and the board ruled as a tyranny: 120 lictors with axes, executions without appeal, refusal to lay down office at the end of the year.

His downfall came through his lust for Verginia, the plebeian centurion's daughter whom he tried to claim as a slave through his client M. Claudius. After Verginius killed her in the Forum and the armies seceded, the decemvirs were forced to abdicate. Verginius, as tribune, prosecuted Appius, who invoked the appeal he had denied others; he was imprisoned and killed himself before trial, or was killed on the tribunes' order.

Livy's Appius is the culmination of a recurring type: the arrogant Claudian patrician who despises the plebs, like his grandfather the consul of 495 and his father the consul of 471. T. P. Wiseman and others have argued that this hostile image of the Claudii was shaped by late Republican annalists, especially Licinius Macer, and by the political quarrels of Clodius' time, and that Appius may have been a reforming figure, author of a law code that many plebeians wanted. Some scholars also suspect that the image of a tyrannical second decemvirate was constructed to explain the unpopular clauses of the last two tables.

M. Furius Camillus dominated Rome in the generation of Veii and the Gallic sack, and Livy called him a second founder of the city. He was censor in 403, consular tribune six times (401, 398, 394, 386, 384, 381) and dictator five times (396, 390, 389, 368, 367). As dictator in 396 he took Veii by tunnelling into its citadel, summoned Juno Regina to Rome by evocatio, and triumphed with four white horses, a sacrilegious imitation of Jupiter that alienated the plebs. In 394 he besieged Falerii; when a schoolmaster led the sons of the leading Faliscans into the Roman camp, Camillus had him stripped and driven back by the boys with rods, and the Faliscans, moved by his good faith, surrendered.

In 391, accused over the Veientine booty, he went into exile at Ardea, praying that Rome would need him. In 390, recalled by a decree carried by messengers through the Gallic lines, he was named dictator, arrived as the ransom was being weighed, declared that Rome would be ransomed with iron, not gold, and destroyed the Gauls. He then persuaded the people not to abandon the ruined city for Veii, in a speech Livy makes a meditation on Rome's sacred places. In the following years he defeated the Volsci at Maecium (389), the Etruscans at Sutrium, the Volsci and Praenestines at Satricum (381), arranged Tusculum's incorporation, and in 367 defeated a Gallic raid near Alba and presided over the Licinio-Sextian compromise, vowing a temple of Concord. He died of plague in 365.

Polybius does not mention him, and the hero of 390 is almost certainly a later elaboration; the miraculous rescue contradicts the versions in which the Gauls left with the gold. Momigliano showed that the Concord vow and much of Camillus' role as reconciler reflect later political ideology. Ancient writers read him as a model for later saviours and Augustus' propaganda drew on him as a refounder. Plutarch wrote his Life, without a Greek pair surviving.

Brennus is the name Roman tradition gave to the leader of the Senonian Gauls who defeated Rome at the Allia and sacked the city in 390 (387/386). Polybius does not name the commander. Livy, Plutarch and Diodorus make him the chieftain who besieged Clusium, demanded the surrender of the Fabian envoys who had violated the law of nations, led the army to the Allia, took the city, and besieged the Capitol for seven months. When the Romans complained that the weights for the ransom of 1,000 pounds of gold were false, he threw his sword onto the scales and said 'vae victis', woe to the vanquished, the phrase by which he is remembered.

In Livy's patriotic version Camillus arrived at that moment and destroyed the Gauls in two battles, killing Brennus' army to a man. Other traditions, preserved by Polybius, Diodorus and Strabo, have the Gauls depart with the gold because the Veneti were raiding their new lands in the Po valley, or be ambushed by the Caeretans on the way home. Justin says the Gauls who sacked Rome then sought alliance with Dionysius of Syracuse, and some may have marched south as mercenaries.

The same name was borne by the leader of the Celtic army that attacked Delphi in 279, which has led some scholars to suggest that 'brennos' was a title or that the Roman tradition borrowed the name from the Greek story. The Senones had settled the Adriatic coast south of Ariminum shortly before, and their grave goods at Montefortino and Filottrano show warriors with Etruscan bronzes and Greek wine services. Brennus became a symbol of barbarian violence in Roman memory, while in 19th-century France he was celebrated as a national hero of Gallic resistance.
